Abstract—Growing rates of crop disease and insect infestations
are threatening the overall health of the agricultural industry
as well as food production worldwide, and traditional methods
for monitoring crops through visual inspection are often too
time-consuming, subjective, and difficult to scale up. This paper
presents an AI-based system capable of diagnosing crop leaf
health in real-time using state-of-the-art computer vision and
deep learning technologies. The framework implemented uses
a multi-step pipeline composed of an object detection model, a
classification model and a vision-based reasoning system; where
the object detection portion of the workflow uses a YOLOv8
model to determine the location of infected areas, an automated
region-of-interest extraction tool is then used to extract from
the image the regions of interest so as to improve the overall
accuracy of disease detection.
2892659e89e30819f2054f587769cd4d.label: NO_CONTRADICTION
2892659e89e30819f2054f587769cd4d.rationale: The two pieces of evidence discuss different topics (ImageNet classification and real-time plant leaf disease detection) and do not provide conflicting information.

f7f487da42215ac4f172fbb997b48ef7.evidence_b:
The earlier methods focused mainly on handcrafted feature
extraction methods where color, texture and shape were the
commonly used features, thus allowing researchers to find
patterns of disease development based on visible character-
istics in plant leaves. Traditional methods provide the ability
to process images quickly; however, traditional methodologies
do not perform well, due to illumination changes, background
interference and large-scale variability characteristics, result-
ing in poor performance in terms of generalisation [20]. With the advent of deep learning, in particular convolutional
neural networks (CNN), the field of plant disease classification
tasks has witnessed remarkable progress. Foundational works
demonstrated that deep CNN architectures are effective in
image recognition, enabling automated feature extraction and
higher classification accuracy [10], [16]. The same models
were used in later studies on agricultural datasets where
promising results were reported in terms of disease identifica-
tion in various types of crops [11], [13] . Transfer learning was
used to boost model performance using pre-trained networks,
reducing the dependence on massive labeled datasets [6], [17]. Recent studies are aimed at developing architectures that
can increase efficiency and accuracy in existing models. The
introduction of compound scaling by EfficientNet have estab-
lished a new paradigm of optimizing depth as well as width &
resolution; leading to superior performance with reduced num-
ber of overall parameters for each model [9]. Research using
EfficientNet for classification of plant diseases have yielded
greater levels of generalization and accuracy than traditional
CNN models [3] .
f7f487da42215ac4f172fbb997b48ef7.label: NO_CONTRADICTION
f7f487da42215ac4f172fbb997b48ef7.rationale: Compatible non-conflicting facts. Evidence A discusses various deep learning models and their applications, while Evidence B discusses the evolution of methods in plant disease classification, highlighting the advancements of deep learning and traditional methods.

are threatening the overall health of the agricultural industry
as well as food production worldwide, and traditional methods
for monitoring crops through visual inspection are often too

Large Language Model (LLM), and asynchronous inference
management. Contrary to the traditional method where the
task of handwritten text recognition and answer assessment is
performed independently, the proposed framework creates an
end-to-end processing pipeline to convert handwritten exami-
nation documents to structured texts for semantic assessment. Evaluation is a multi-stage process that starts from scanning
of question papers and handwritten answer sheets in PDF
or image format.

The automated evaluation of handwritten descriptive an-

intersection of computer vision, natural language processing,
and educational technology. In earlier Automated Essay Scor-
ing (AES) systems, the use of lexical features and manu-
ally crafted rules was predominant which prevented them
from assessing semantic comprehension. Recent progress in
Vision-Language Models (VLMs), handwriting recognition,
and Large Language Models (LLMs) has made it possible
to improve document understanding and semantic evaluation
significantly. However, current techniques do not integrate
the tasks of handwriting recognition and answer evaluation,
taking into account examination specific constraints and rubric
based evaluation. This work tries to overcome this problem by
providing an integrated system for the end-to-end evaluation
of handwritten descriptive answer scripts. A. Automated Essay and Answer-Sheet Scoring with NLP and
LLMs
First-generation AES systems made use of lexical prop-
erties, rules designed by humans, and keyword matching
for mimicking human evaluation [1], [14]. While efficient
from the computational point of view, these methods did not
have the capacity to incorporate semantic comprehension and
conceptual accuracy [13]. Syntactic and linguistic features
used in machine learning algorithms enhanced consistency of
scoring yet were task-specific and lacked generalizability [6],
[15], [18]. The introduction of Transformer-based language models has
greatly contributed to the automation of assessment via contex-
tual semantic reasoning.

Abstract—Evaluation of handwritten descriptive answer scripts
has always been considered difficult due to handwriting differ-
ences, OCR errors, semantics variability of students’ answers,
and specific rules for grading in the particular examination pro-
cess. The existing approaches to automated assessments mainly
involve using the clean digital version of text and lexical matching
techniques, restricting their application in real-life scenarios
of handwritten examinations. This paper proposes an end-to-
end AI-powered system that combines Vision-Language Optical
Character Recognition (OCR) and constraint-aware Large Lan-
guage Model (LLM) in order to provide semantic grading of
handwritten answer scripts.
11b8edf9a1e71964992200aa46ed08cf.evidence_b:
A Florence-2 vision-language model
that was fine-tuned on the IAM Handwriting Database is used
for recognizing handwritten texts in a reliable way followed
by an answer alignment algorithm that aligns the answers to
questions considering the peculiarities of the examination process
structure. The grading is performed by locally running Llama
3 (8B) grading engine that evaluates the answers according to
the grading rubrics, including the marking scheme, optional
questions, and section-wise grading. Index Terms—Automated Essay Scoring (AES), Handwritten
Text Recognition, Vision-Language Models, Florence-2, Large
Language Models, Semantic Answer Assessment, Constraint-
Aware Grading, Educational AI. I. INTRODUCTION
Descriptive tests through handwriting still form one of the
main methods of evaluating the students’ conceptual knowl-
edge, analytical skills, and problem-solving skills in education
centers. Nonetheless, manual assessment of such handwritten
answer papers involves intensive work, delays, and is always
subjective, leading to inconsistent scoring and late posting
of the results. As the number of students keeps increasing,
there is an increased need for intelligent automated systems
for conducting assessments [1], [14], [16]. The latest developments in NLP, VLMs, and LLMs have
greatly enhanced Automated Essay Scoring and document
understanding [5], [10], [18]. However, most AES tools are
designed for digitally typed texts or make use of lexical
matching and thus do not apply to handwritten descriptive
exams where variations in handwriting styles, OCR mistakes,
and different ways of writing an answer continue to be a
problem [1], [9], [13].

The automated evaluation of handwritten descriptive an-
swer scripts is an important research topic that lies at the
intersection of computer vision, natural language processing,
and educational technology. In earlier Automated Essay Scor-
ing (AES) systems, the use of lexical features and manu-
ally crafted rules was predominant which prevented them
from assessing semantic comprehension. Recent progress in
Vision-Language Models (VLMs), handwriting recognition,
and Large Language Models (LLMs) has made it possible
to improve document understanding and semantic evaluation
significantly. However, current techniques do not integrate
the tasks of handwriting recognition and answer evaluation,
taking into account examination specific constraints and rubric
based evaluation. This work tries to overcome this problem by
providing an integrated system for the end-to-end evaluation
of handwritten descriptive answer scripts. A. Automated Essay and Answer-Sheet Scoring with NLP and
LLMs
First-generation AES systems made use of lexical prop-
erties, rules designed by humans, and keyword matching
for mimicking human evaluation [1], [14]. While efficient
from the computational point of view, these methods did not
have the capacity to incorporate semantic comprehension and
conceptual accuracy [13]. Syntactic and linguistic features
used in machine learning algorithms enhanced consistency of
scoring yet were task-specific and lacked generalizability [6],
[15], [18]. The introduction of Transformer-based language models has
greatly contributed to the automation of assessment via contex-
tual semantic reasoning.

been shown to exhibit high agreement with human assessors
[4], [10], [12], and the recent use of LLaMA-based models
has facilitated rubric-driven assessment via semantic analysis
and explanation [2], [7], [8]. Nevertheless, existing grading systems based on LLMs
make use of digitized data [5], [16] and disregard problems
associated with handwriting. Errors in OCR adversely affect
subsequent analysis on the semantic level, thereby decreasing
the accuracy of grading. In spite of the fact that some recent
works have considered multi-modal handwritten answer sheet
assessment [20], Vision-Language OCR with constraint-aware
LLM grading has not been sufficiently studied yet. B. Vision-Language Models for Handwritten Document Un-
derstanding

continues to be a key problem in automated educational assess-
ment because of differences in handwriting, document quality,
and page layout complexity. Traditional HTR systems yielded
encouraging results on standard datasets such as the IAM
Handwriting Database [13], [18], although their effectiveness

As OCR quality
influences the quality of semantic grading, recognition quality
was examined in terms of handwriting style diversity and
implementation features [20]. The optimized Florence-2 system was benchmarked against
Tesseract OCR, CRNN-CTC, TrOCR Base, and Groq Vision
API based on Character Error Rate (CER), off-line operation,
and multimodal document understanding [16], [20]. The experimental results show that the suggested Florence-
2 model exhibits comparable OCR accuracy, with the capacity
to deploy in an offline setting and to process multimodal docu-
ments. This contrasts with traditional OCR systems that focus
on text recognition or cloud services that require connectivity,
and it offers a secure and private solution for evaluating hand-
written answers [13], [18], [20]. The quantitative comparison
of the evaluated OCR models is presented in Table II. Table II demonstrates that Florence-2 is a multimodal docu-
ment understanding system which, at the same time, provides
high recognition accuracy and offline operation. Although
Tesseract OCR, CRNN-CTC, and TrOCR Base offer offline
inference but not multimodality, Groq Vision API offers mul-
timodal reasoning but requires cloud connectivity. Thus, the
proposed Florence-2 system can be used effectively for offline
handwriting evaluation. B. Semantic Grading Performance
To test the semantic grading capabilities of the proposed
framework, experiments were carried out by comparing the
OCR-extracted answers of students with the answers provided
by the instructor with the help of Llama 3 grading module. Un-
like traditional methods which work on the basis of keyword
matching, language models conduct semantic evaluation by
evaluating the concepts instead of matching lexical forms [5],
[10], [18].

Abstract—Evaluation of handwritten descriptive answer scripts
has always been considered difficult due to handwriting differ-
ences, OCR errors, semantics variability of students’ answers,
and specific rules for grading in the particular examination pro-
cess. The existing approaches to automated assessments mainly
involve using the clean digital version of text and lexical matching
techniques, restricting their application in real-life scenarios
of handwritten examinations. This paper proposes an end-to-
end AI-powered system that combines Vision-Language Optical
Character Recognition (OCR) and constraint-aware Large Lan-
guage Model (LLM) in order to provide semantic grading of
handwritten answer scripts.

of the evaluated OCR models is presented in Table II. Table II demonstrates that Florence-2 is a multimodal docu-
ment understanding system which, at the same time, provides
high recognition accuracy and offline operation. Although
Tesseract OCR, CRNN-CTC, and TrOCR Base offer offline
inference but not multimodality, Groq Vision API offers mul-
timodal reasoning but requires cloud connectivity. Thus, the
proposed Florence-2 system can be used effectively for offline
handwriting evaluation. B. Semantic Grading Performance
To test the semantic grading capabilities of the proposed
framework, experiments were carried out by comparing the
OCR-extracted answers of students with the answers provided
by the instructor with the help of Llama 3 grading module. Un-
like traditional methods which work on the basis of keyword
matching, language models conduct semantic evaluation by
evaluating the concepts instead of matching lexical forms [5],
[10], [18].

matching, language models conduct semantic evaluation by
evaluating the concepts instead of matching lexical forms [5],

A Florence-2 vision-language model
that was fine-tuned on the IAM Handwriting Database is used
for recognizing handwritten texts in a reliable way followed
by an answer alignment algorithm that aligns the answers to
questions considering the peculiarities of the examination process
structure. The grading is performed by locally running Llama
3 (8B) grading engine that evaluates the answers according to
the grading rubrics, including the marking scheme, optional
questions, and section-wise grading. Index Terms—Automated Essay Scoring (AES), Handwritten
Text Recognition, Vision-Language Models, Florence-2, Large
Language Models, Semantic Answer Assessment, Constraint-
Aware Grading, Educational AI. I. INTRODUCTION
Descriptive tests through handwriting still form one of the
main methods of evaluating the students’ conceptual knowl-
edge, analytical skills, and problem-solving skills in education
centers. Nonetheless, manual assessment of such handwritten
answer papers involves intensive work, delays, and is always
subjective, leading to inconsistent scoring and late posting
of the results. As the number of students keeps increasing,
there is an increased need for intelligent automated systems
for conducting assessments [1], [14], [16]. The latest developments in NLP, VLMs, and LLMs have
greatly enhanced Automated Essay Scoring and document
understanding [5], [10], [18]. However, most AES tools are
designed for digitally typed texts or make use of lexical
matching and thus do not apply to handwritten descriptive
exams where variations in handwriting styles, OCR mistakes,
and different ways of writing an answer continue to be a
problem [1], [9], [13].

The automated evaluation of handwritten descriptive an-
swer scripts is an important research topic that lies at the
intersection of computer vision, natural language processing,
and educational technology. In earlier Automated Essay Scor-
ing (AES) systems, the use of lexical features and manu-
ally crafted rules was predominant which prevented them
from assessing semantic comprehension. Recent progress in
Vision-Language Models (VLMs), handwriting recognition,
and Large Language Models (LLMs) has made it possible
to improve document understanding and semantic evaluation
significantly. However, current techniques do not integrate
the tasks of handwriting recognition and answer evaluation,
taking into account examination specific constraints and rubric
based evaluation. This work tries to overcome this problem by
providing an integrated system for the end-to-end evaluation
of handwritten descriptive answer scripts. A. Automated Essay and Answer-Sheet Scoring with NLP and
LLMs
First-generation AES systems made use of lexical prop-
erties, rules designed by humans, and keyword matching
for mimicking human evaluation [1], [14]. While efficient
from the computational point of view, these methods did not
have the capacity to incorporate semantic comprehension and
conceptual accuracy [13]. Syntactic and linguistic features
used in machine learning algorithms enhanced consistency of
scoring yet were task-specific and lacked generalizability [6],
[15], [18]. The introduction of Transformer-based language models has
greatly contributed to the automation of assessment via contex-
tual semantic reasoning.

claims.text: Evaluation of handwritten descriptive answer scripts has always been considered difficult due to handwriting differences, OCR errors, semantics variability of students’ answers, and specific rules for grading in the particular examination process.

The existing approaches to automated assessments mainly involve using the clean digital version of text and lexical matching techniques, restricting their application in real-life scenarios of handwritten examinations.

This paper proposes an end-to-end AI-powered system that combines Vision-Language Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and constraint-aware Large Language Model (LLM) in order to provide semantic grading of handwritten answer scripts.
The system combines dense retrieval using Model X with sparse retrieval using BM25.
The results are fused using RRF.

Experiments
We experiment with RAG in a wide range of knowledge-intensive tasks. For all experiments, we use
a single Wikipedia dump for our non-parametric knowledge source. Following Lee et al. [31] and
Karpukhin et al. [26], we use the December 2018 dump. Each Wikipedia article is split into disjoint
100-word chunks, to make a total of 21M documents. We use the document encoder to compute an
embedding for each document, and build a single MIPS index using FAISS [23] with a Hierarchical
Navigable Small World approximation for fast retrieval [37]. During training, we retrieve the top
k documents for each query. We consider k ∈{5, 10} for training and set k for test time using dev
data. We now discuss experimental details for each task.
3.1
Open-domain Question Answering
Open-domain question answering (QA) is an important real-world application and common testbed
for knowledge-intensive tasks [20]. We treat questions and answers as input-output text pairs (x, y)
and train RAG by directly minimizing the negative log-likelihood of answers. We compare RAG to
the popular extractive QA paradigm [5, 7, 31, 26], where answers are extracted spans from retrieved
documents, relying primarily on non-parametric knowledge. We also compare to “Closed-Book
QA” approaches [52], which, like RAG, generate answers, but which do not exploit retrieval, instead
relying purely on parametric knowledge. We consider four popular open-domain QA datasets: Natural
Questions (NQ) [29], TriviaQA (TQA) [24]. WebQuestions (WQ) [3] and CuratedTrec (CT) [2].

Prior work on general-purpose architectures for NLP
tasks has shown great success without the use of retrieval. A single, pre-trained language model
has been shown to achieve strong performance on various classiﬁcation tasks in the GLUE bench-
marks [60, 61] after ﬁne-tuning [49, 8]. GPT-2 [50] later showed that a single, left-to-right, pre-trained
language model could achieve strong performance across both discriminative and generative tasks. For further improvement, BART [32] and T5 [51, 52] propose a single, pre-trained encoder-decoder
model that leverages bi-directional attention to achieve stronger performance on discriminative
and generative tasks. Our work aims to expand the space of possible tasks with a single, uniﬁed
architecture, by learning a retrieval module to augment pre-trained, generative language models. Learned Retrieval
There is signiﬁcant work on learning to retrieve documents in information
retrieval, more recently with pre-trained, neural language models [44, 26] similar to ours. Some
work optimizes the retrieval module to aid in a speciﬁc, downstream task such as question answering,
using search [46], reinforcement learning [6, 63, 62], or a latent variable approach [31, 20] as in our
work. These successes leverage different retrieval-based architectures and optimization techniques to
achieve strong performance on a single task, while we show that a single retrieval-based architecture
can be ﬁne-tuned for strong performance on a variety of tasks. Memory-based Architectures
Our document index can be seen as a large external memory for
neural networks to attend to, analogous to memory networks [64, 55].

Retrieval Collapse
In preliminary experiments, we observed that for some tasks such as story generation [11], the
retrieval component would “collapse” and learn to retrieve the same documents regardless of the
input. In these cases, once retrieval had collapsed, the generator would learn to ignore the documents,
and the RAG model would perform equivalently to BART. The collapse could be due to a less-explicit
requirement for factual knowledge in some tasks, or the longer target sequences, which could result
in less informative gradients for the retriever.

VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
In this paper, an AI-based Sleep Apnea Detection Sys-
tem has been presented, which analyzes electrocardiogram
(ECG) signals and uses machine learning algorithms for non-
invasive and automatic apnea detection. This system is able to
distinguish between normal and apneic breathing patterns by
extracting twelve time and statistical features from 30 second
ECG segments. Among the classifiers tested – Random For-
est, SVM, Logistic Regression, and MLP, the Random For-
est classifier delivered the most accurate results in terms of
accuracy, F1-score, and ROC-AUC [3], [9], [10]. Besides the high accuracy rate, the system stresses inter-
pretability, efficiency, and clinical applicability. While deep
learning models depend on extensive training data and com-
putational power, this feature extraction technique provides
a more efficient, transparent, and deployable method. Em-
bedding the trained model into an interactive Streamlit web
applica- tion increases its usability, enabling healthcare work-
ers to up- load ECG signals, view the findings, and produce
clinical re- ports instantly. Therefore, this system is a viable
tool for sleep apnea pre-screening [14], [15].

Abstract—Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) is a highly danger-
ous sleep disorder that needs efficient and affordable methods of
diagnosis apart from complicated polysomnography procedures. This paper presents a machine learning approach for automatic
detection of sleep apnea events based on single lead ECG
records from the Apnea-ECG database on the PhysioNet site. The
proposed methodology includes pre-processing of ECG records
to extract the heart wave pattern’s time domain features. These
normalized features are then used to train a few supervised
machine learning classifiers, such as Random Forest, Support
Vector Machine (SVM), Logistic Regression, and Multi-Layer
Perceptron (MLP).

II. LITERATURE REVIEW
Automatic sleep apnea detection using physiological sig-
nals has attracted significant research attention because of
its potential to provide an affordable and non-invasive al-
ternative to conventional polysomnography (PSG) [10], [13]. Although PSG remains the clinical gold standard for diag-
nosing obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), it requires overnight
monitoring in specialized laboratories, expensive equipment,
and trained medical personnel, making it unsuitable for large-
scale screening [13]. Consequently, researchers have explored
alternative physiological signals such as electrocardiogram
(ECG), oxygen saturation (SpO2), respiratory effort, and heart
rate variability (HRV) to develop automated and accessible
diagnostic systems [2], [3], [5], [15]. Early ECG-based approaches primarily relied on hand-
crafted time-domain and frequency-domain features extracted
from cardiac signals. Variations in R-R intervals, heart rate
variability, and ECG morphology were shown to correlate
strongly with apnea episodes, demonstrating the feasibility
of ECG as a standalone signal for sleep apnea detection [2],
[3], [6], [12], [13]. Subsequently, advanced signal processing
techniques such as wavelet transforms, spectral entropy, and
frequency-domain analysis were introduced to improve the
characterization of transient physiological changes associated
with apnea events [2], [3], [6]. With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, ma-
chine learning has become a widely adopted approach for
automated sleep apnea detection.

VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
In this paper, an AI-based Sleep Apnea Detection Sys-
tem has been presented, which analyzes electrocardiogram
(ECG) signals and uses machine learning algorithms for non-
invasive and automatic apnea detection. This system is able to
distinguish between normal and apneic breathing patterns by
extracting twelve time and statistical features from 30 second
ECG segments. Among the classifiers tested – Random For-
est, SVM, Logistic Regression, and MLP, the Random For-
est classifier delivered the most accurate results in terms of
accuracy, F1-score, and ROC-AUC [3], [9], [10]. Besides the high accuracy rate, the system stresses inter-
pretability, efficiency, and clinical applicability. While deep
learning models depend on extensive training data and com-
putational power, this feature extraction technique provides
a more efficient, transparent, and deployable method. Em-
bedding the trained model into an interactive Streamlit web
applica- tion increases its usability, enabling healthcare work-
ers to up- load ECG signals, view the findings, and produce
clinical re- ports instantly. Therefore, this system is a viable
tool for sleep apnea pre-screening [14], [15].

ous sleep disorder that needs efficient and affordable methods of
diagnosis apart from complicated polysomnography procedures. This paper presents a machine learning approach for automatic
detection of sleep apnea events based on single lead ECG
records from the Apnea-ECG database on the PhysioNet site. The
proposed methodology includes pre-processing of ECG records
to extract the heart wave pattern’s time domain features. These
normalized features are then used to train a few supervised
machine learning classifiers, such as Random Forest, Support
Vector Machine (SVM), Logistic Regression, and Multi-Layer
Perceptron (MLP).

Abstract—Evaluation of handwritten descriptive answer scripts
has always been considered difficult due to handwriting differ-
ences, OCR errors, semantics variability of students’ answers,
and specific rules for grading in the particular examination pro-
cess. The existing approaches to automated assessments mainly
involve using the clean digital version of text and lexical matching
techniques, restricting their application in real-life scenarios
of handwritten examinations. This paper proposes an end-to-
end AI-powered system that combines Vision-Language Optical
Character Recognition (OCR) and constraint-aware Large Lan-
guage Model (LLM) in order to provide semantic grading of
handwritten answer scripts.

has always been considered difficult due to handwriting differ-
ences, OCR errors, semantics variability of students’ answers,
and specific rules for grading in the particular examination pro-

involve using the clean digital version of text and lexical matching
techniques, restricting their application in real-life scenarios
of handwritten examinations. This paper proposes an end-to-
end AI-powered system that combines Vision-Language Optical
Character Recognition (OCR) and constraint-aware Large Lan-
guage Model (LLM) in order to provide semantic grading of
handwritten answer scripts.

This framework was implemented in a modular and offline-
first design to guarantee a reliable and scalable evaluation
of handwritten descriptive answers scripts. The framework
incorporates three main modules: Vision-Language OCR, se-
mantic grading with constraints, and asynchronous inference

coordinating the entire process from the preprocessing of the
documents to OCR detection, semantic analysis, and the man-
agement of the results using an execution pipeline. The model
used for handwritten text extraction is called Florence-2. The
local deployment of Llama 3, using Ollama, is responsible
for semantic analysis without the need for any cloud-based
services [19], [20]. The framework utilizes an asynchronous queue to schedule
OCR and LLM inference tasks separately to ensure no GPU
contention occurs during simultaneous operations. Results, text
output, and metadata are permanently stored in an efficient
and lightweight SQLite database for efficient retrieval, result
tracking, and management. This makes the design flexible
enough such that the different modules can work separately
but in a coherent manner to accommodate future incorporation
of other OCR and LLM models or grading techniques [16]. V. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

answer papers involves intensive work, delays, and is always
subjective, leading to inconsistent scoring and late posting

for conducting assessments [1], [14], [16]. The latest developments in NLP, VLMs, and LLMs have
greatly enhanced Automated Essay Scoring and document
understanding [5], [10], [18]. However, most AES tools are
designed for digitally typed texts or make use of lexical
matching and thus do not apply to handwritten descriptive
exams where variations in handwriting styles, OCR mistakes,

problem [1], [9], [13].

processing multiple answer scripts at the same time may cause

the use of asynchronous queuing scheduling approach by the
proposed framework which will process answer scripts one by
one. Every uploaded answer script is queued for evaluation and
graded independently using the OCR module and semantic
grading module. This sequential scheduling avoids any conflict
in GPU inference, optimizes the usage of resources, and allows
the batch processing of handwritten answer scripts. Once the evaluation is completed, the output text, evaluation
outcomes, and metadata are stored in a SQLite database per-
manently.

claims.text: Each ECG recording is segmented into 30-second windows with 50% overlap.
The 30-second windows are used to effectively capture variations during apnea events.

Twelve time-domain features are extracted from each segment, including signal energy, RMS, zero-crossing rate (ZCR), heart rate variability (HRV), and descriptive statistics such as mean, median, minimum, maximum, and percentiles.

III. DATASET
The data that is taken into account in this research is the
Apnea-ECG Database, which has been made available through
PhysioNet [13]. The data consist of ECG recordings of patients
that are suffering from sleep apnea as well as the ones that
are not suffering from it, and there are also events annotated
to pinpoint the occurrences of apnea. The database, being
clinical relevant and having both ECG signals and expert
labels, is mostly used for research aimed at automatic sleep
apnea diagnosis [2], [3], [10]. A. Data Collection
The collection consists of 70 long-duration ECG recordings
which were taken at 100 Hz frequency [13]. Within each
recording, there exist a number of ECG signal segments that
have been noted with apnea events by experts. The annotations
are in .apn files, where each event is classified according to
its severity (e.g., normal respiration or apnea). Apnea events
would usually mean short periods of abnormal heart activity
caused by breathing patterns stopping during sleep [10], [11].

III. DATASET
The data that is taken into account in this research is the
Apnea-ECG Database, which has been made available through
PhysioNet [13]. The data consist of ECG recordings of patients
that are suffering from sleep apnea as well as the ones that
are not suffering from it, and there are also events annotated
to pinpoint the occurrences of apnea. The database, being
clinical relevant and having both ECG signals and expert
labels, is mostly used for research aimed at automatic sleep
apnea diagnosis [2], [3], [10]. A. Data Collection
The collection consists of 70 long-duration ECG recordings
which were taken at 100 Hz frequency [13]. Within each
recording, there exist a number of ECG signal segments that
have been noted with apnea events by experts. The annotations
are in .apn files, where each event is classified according to
its severity (e.g., normal respiration or apnea). Apnea events
would usually mean short periods of abnormal heart activity
caused by breathing patterns stopping during sleep [10], [11].
